exercise.name: Reverse Crunch

reference.title: Reverse Crunch
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Body weight, exercise type Strength

exercise.mechanics: Compound (posterior pelvic tilt and lumbar flexion, hips flexed)

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl the hips up, inhale as you lower slowly.
breathing.cadence: About 1.2 s up, short pause, about 2 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1 s up, brief pause, 2 s down; no swinging
prescription.progression: Slower lowering, then on a decline bench, then hanging knee raises

cues.text: Lie on your back, arms by your sides palms down, hips and knees bent about 90 degrees (shins level).
Breathe out and curl the hips off the mat, bringing the knees toward the chest. Lift with the abs, not a leg swing.
Pause briefly with the tailbone off the mat; shoulders and head stay down.
Breathe in and roll the pelvis down slowly, one vertebra at a time, back to 90/90.
Keep the knee angle fixed; repeat without dropping the legs.

mistakes.fix: Slow down; curl the pelvis up and lower for about 2 s.
Hands rest lightly for balance; the abs lift the hips.

mistakes.mistake: Opening the knees on the way down (legs drop toward the floor)
mistakes.fix: Keep the knees bent about 90 degrees and stop when the thighs are vertical.
Lift only the pelvis and low back; the shoulder blades stay on the mat.

kinematics.norm: Pelvis curls up until the tailbone and low back peel off the mat (clinical opinion)
Low back curls; no study reports the angle (clinical opinion)
Thighs vertical at the start (hips about 90 degrees), knees drawn toward the chest at the top (clinical opinion)
Pelvis rises a few centimetres off the mat; the upper back stays down (clinical opinion)
About 1 s up, 2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: Escamilla et al. 2006, electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises (Phys Ther 86(5):656-671)
Sarti et al. 1996, muscle activity in upper and lower rectus abdominis during abdominal exercises (Arch Phys Med Rehabil 77(12):1293-1297; PMID 8976314)
Clark, Holt and Sinyard 2003, electromyographic comparison of the upper and lower rectus abdominis during abdominal exercises (J Strength Cond Res 17(3):475-483; PMID 12930172)
Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
An electromyographic analysis of the Ab-Slide exercise, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust and side bridge in healthy young adults (J Strength Cond Res 22(6):1939-1946; PMID 18978615)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.

Low-back pain, disc problems or flexion intolerance: start with a McGill-style curl-up, dead bug or plank; partial curl-ups gave the best abdominal challenge for the least spine compression in one model study (Axler and McGill 1997).
Hip-flexor heavy variants (inclined reverse crunch) gave high rectus femoris activity, which may not suit some people with low-back problems (Escamilla 2006).
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion or straight-leg work.
modify: Low-back discomfort: smaller curl (tailbone just off the mat) or a posterior pelvic tilt with feet on the floor.
Neck tension: relax the head on the mat.
regressions: Posterior pelvic tilt with feet on the floor.
Reverse crunch with feet tapping the floor between reps.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the pelvis toward the ribs. A reverse crunch on a 30-degree incline was among the highest upper and lower rectus activations tested (Escamilla 2006); on the flat floor a reverse curl-up gave less rectus activity than a curl-up (Clark 2003). A posterior pelvic tilt worked the lower rectus harder than a curl-up in trained people (Sarti 1996).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Internal obliques were highly active in the inclined reverse crunch (Escamilla 2006); the obliques also steady the pelvis as it rolls.
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Internal obliques were highly active in the inclined reverse crunch (Escamilla 2006); the obliques also steady the pelvis as it rolls.
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Hold the thighs up at about 90 degrees and bring the knees in; they should not swing the legs. The aim is the pelvis curl, not more hip flexion.
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Hold the thighs up at about 90 degrees and bring the knees in; they should not swing the legs. The aim is the pelvis curl, not more hip flexion.
muscleNotes.quads_r: Rectus femoris works as a hip flexor: its activity was high in the inclined reverse crunch (Escamilla 2006), which the authors flagged for people with low-back problems.
muscleNotes.quads_l: Rectus femoris works as a hip flexor: its activity was high in the inclined reverse crunch (Escamilla 2006), which the authors flagged for people with low-back problems.

guides.label: Pelvis curls up and back down
